title: Stream Processing & Windowing
summary: Turning an unbounded stream into aggregates by defining a window of time to aggregate over, and what happens when events arrive late.

slides.markdown:
Counting, summing, or averaging over a stream sounds simple until you ask: over what period? A stream never ends, so "the average" has no answer unless you first bound it into a window of time.

This topic covers the three ways to define that window — tumbling, sliding, session — and the harder problem underneath all of them: events don't always arrive in the order they happened, so a stream processor needs a rule for deciding when a window is finally done.

slides.sectionTitle: Why you can't aggregate an infinite stream without first bounding it somehow
slides.markdown:
A batch job over a finite table can compute "total orders" once and be done. A stream of order events never stops arriving, so "total orders" isn't a single number — it's a number that keeps changing forever, and "average order value" is meaningless without saying *average over what*.

This is the core problem **windowing** solves: it slices an unbounded stream into bounded chunks, like "orders in the last 5 minutes" or "clicks in this user's current session," so an aggregate actually has a well-defined answer at any point in time.

Every stream-processing system, whether Kafka Streams, Flink, or Spark Structured Streaming, builds its aggregation model around windows for exactly this reason — you can't sum an infinite [log-based](log-based-streaming) stream, but you can sum a well-defined slice of it, repeatedly, as the stream flows through.

slides.sectionTitle: Tumbling windows: fixed, non-overlapping time buckets
slides.markdown:
A **tumbling window** slices time into fixed-size, back-to-back, non-overlapping buckets — 00:00-00:05, 00:05-00:10, 00:10-00:15, and so on. Every event belongs to exactly one window, based on its timestamp.

This is the natural fit for a metric like "orders per 5-minute interval" on a dashboard: each bucket produces one final number once it closes, and buckets never share data, so summing across buckets just gives you the total for the combined period with no double-counting.

The trade-off: a tumbling window only reports once per bucket, so a metric computed this way updates in discrete steps, every 5 minutes, rather than continuously.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: tumbling vs sliding vs session windows over the same event stream
slides.markdown:
![The same event stream shown as tumbling windows (fixed, non-overlapping), sliding windows (fixed, overlapping), and session windows (variable length, separated by activity gaps)](assets/window-types.svg)

Tumbling and sliding both use a fixed clock-time width, but sliding windows overlap — the same event can fall inside several sliding windows at once, unlike tumbling, where each event belongs to exactly one bucket.

Session windows are the odd one out: their boundaries aren't fixed by the clock at all, they're defined by the data itself — a gap in activity longer than some threshold ends the session, so window length varies from one stretch of events to the next.

assets.alt: The same event stream shown as tumbling windows (fixed, non-overlapping), sliding windows (fixed, overlapping), and session windows (variable length, separated by activity gaps)

slides.sectionTitle: Sliding windows: overlapping buckets for a "last N minutes" style metric
slides.markdown:
A **sliding window** also has a fixed width, but it moves forward continuously, or in small steps, rather than jumping to the next non-overlapping bucket — "the last 5 minutes, recalculated every 30 seconds" is a sliding window with a 5-minute width and a 30-second slide.

This fits a "trending now" style metric: a moving average of requests per second, recalculated frequently, where you want a smooth, continuously updated number rather than one fresh reading every 5 minutes.

The cost is that a single event can be counted in multiple overlapping windows — this is by design, it's what makes the metric smooth, but it means sliding-window aggregates aren't additive the way tumbling windows are; you can't safely sum two overlapping windows to get a combined total.

slides.sectionTitle: Session windows: grouped by activity gaps instead of fixed time
slides.markdown:
A **session window** groups events by a gap in activity rather than by clock time: a user's clicks all belong to the same session as long as no click is followed by, say, 30+ minutes of silence — the next click after a gap that long starts a brand-new session.

This fits "how long did this user's browsing session last" or "how many pages did they view in one visit" — questions where the natural boundary is behavioral, not a fixed clock interval, and where session length genuinely varies, a 2-minute bounce vs a 45-minute deep browse.

Unlike tumbling or sliding windows, a session window's boundaries aren't known in advance — the processor has to wait to see whether the gap threshold has actually been exceeded before it can finalize where a session ended.

slides.sectionTitle: Event time vs processing time, and why late-arriving events break naive windowing
slides.markdown:
**Event time** is when something actually happened, a click at 10:00:03 on the user's device; **processing time** is when the stream processor actually receives and handles that event, maybe 10:00:09, after some network delay. They're rarely identical, and the gap between them isn't fixed — it varies with network conditions, retries, and backlog.

If you window naively by processing time, a burst of network delay can shove a batch of 10:00:00-ish events into the 10:00:10 window instead of the 10:00:00 window they actually belong to, silently corrupting both windows' counts.

Correct windowing groups by **event time** whenever the business question is about when things actually happened, which is most of the time, but that immediately raises a new problem: a processor can't know a window is "done" just because its clock passed the window's end, since a late event time-stamped for that window might still be in flight. That's the problem watermarks exist to answer, and it's the same event-time-vs-arrival gap that makes [ordering across a distributed system](time-and-ordering) hard in general.

slides.sectionTitle: Watermarks: a stream processor's way of deciding "late enough that we close the window"
slides.markdown:
A **watermark** is the stream processor's declared estimate of "I don't expect to see any more events with an event-time earlier than this." When the watermark passes a window's end time, the processor closes that window and emits its final result, even though, technically, a straggling event could still arrive after that.

Setting the watermark is a genuine trade-off: a tight watermark, closing windows quickly, gives fast results but risks dropping or mishandling truly late events; a loose watermark, waiting longer, handles stragglers better but delays every window's result, even for data that was never going to be late.

Most systems let you configure this as "allowed lateness," a grace period after the watermark passes during which a late event can still update an already-emitted window, at the cost of occasionally correcting a number you already reported.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: windowing choice by use case — dashboards (tumbling), trending (sliding), user sessions (session)
slides.markdown:
| | Tumbling | Sliding | Session |
|---|---|---|
| Boundaries | Fixed, non-overlapping | Fixed width, overlapping | Variable, defined by activity gaps |
| Update frequency | Once per bucket | Continuously (per slide interval) | Once the session's gap threshold is exceeded |
| Good fit | Dashboards: "orders per 5 minutes" | Trending metrics: "requests/sec, last 5 min" | User behavior: "pages per browsing session" |
| Additive across windows? | Yes | No — windows overlap | No — windows vary in length |

**How to decide:** ask what the number is actually *for*. A fixed reporting cadence wants tumbling; a smooth, continuously updated trend wants sliding; a question about one user's continuous activity wants session.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: windowing by processing time and getting wrong counts whenever consumers fall behind
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'll just window by the time my server received each event — simpler than dealing with event-time timestamps."

**Why it's wrong:** if consumers fall behind during a load spike, a burst of events that all *happened* around 10:00:00 might not get *processed* until 10:00:45 — windowing by processing time puts them all in the 10:00:45 window, silently inflating that window's count and leaving the 10:00:00 window's count too low, even though nothing was actually lost.

**Correct model:** window by event time whenever the question is about when things happened, and use watermarks to decide when a window can safely close — processing-time windowing is only safe when processing time and event time are guaranteed to stay tightly in sync, which a system under load can't promise.
